newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Zinc price squeezed to seven-year high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Zinc price squeezed to seven-year high.

text.p: Zinc surged to its highest for seven years on Friday as a market squeeze extended a rally that pulled along other industrial metals in its slipstream.
Speculative buying lifted aluminium, copper and nickel.
"Once one metal gets going, the euphoria tends to spill over," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis

Three months zinc touched $1,625 per tonne, bringing gains over the past two days to $100 and the month's rise to $204, or 14 percent. Zinc ended the day $53 higher at $1,624 on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
Analysts see the next important target $100 higher. "It has got to get through $1,700," said Jim Lennon of Macquarie Bank.
Zinc is mainly in demand for galvanising steel, but the current rally is based more or market action than consumer interest.
Chinese producers with big short positions have been caught on the wrong side of the sudden rise, and may have to buy up to 200,000 tonnes of zinc to square their positions, according to Lennon.
Chinese smelters were reported by China Metals magazine to be short by up to 250,000 tonnes of zinc, and since the end of 1996 only 38,000 tonnes have been put into Singapore warehouses.
"The Chinese producers overestimated how much they could produce and what is of deliverable quality for the LME," Williamson said.

Delays in obtaining further export permits by China National Non-Ferrous Metals Corporation, which has already reached its export limits for 1997, may force the Chinese producers to buy around 200,000 tonnes on the market to offset short positions, Lennon said.

Producers were not able to sell at current levels since industrial consumers were not willing to buy and some were even running down stocks. Consumers were said to be waiting for a downward correction before buying.
Prices for the second half of 1998 average $1,330 while cash prices are so much higher.
"There is no opportunity to lock in any reasonable price. Producers cannot really capitalise," Lennon said. "It is a classic squeeze."

"It is not that surprising there has been a price rise," said Paul White of the International Lead and Zinc Study Group (ILZSG). He added that sentiment and fundamentals were both strong, and western consumption was expected to be up 5-1/2 percent this year.
A deficit of 200,000 tonnes was forecast by ILZSG for this year, the same as in 1996.
Others were more sceptical, and brokers were nervous of being caught on the wrong side of any correction.
Prices in other world commodity markets were mostly little changed from Thursday.
